identifies_rows: The KEY identifies a row. The id (R1, R2, ...) is assigned by position in this file and means nothing outside it.
instructions: your_value -- the number the source states. If sources disagree, give the range AND the rule you used to reduce it (for example "2.5-2.7, took the midpoint to two significant figures").
source -- the authority you consulted, specific enough to find again.

citation_correct -- about the code's cited source only, carried on each row as "cited". Answer it separately from the value: a right number under a wrong authority is a real finding and one token cannot say it.
notes -- anything a token cannot carry. The checker reads notes as prose for a human, never as a verdict.

One token per verdict field. A field holding a token plus a qualification is reported as unclassified rather than read, because guessing which half you meant is the interpretation this system is built to avoid.
row_hash: sha256 over key, claim and code value, first 8 hex characters. Do not edit those three fields; the checker recomputes this and a row whose hash is missing or wrong is returned rather than read.
selection_why: constants_new.py only -- the pilot slice (L-201). Its branch coverage is a property of the file, not of anyone's judgement about which rows are interesting.

cited: IAU 2012 Resolution B2 -- exact definition
notes: Exact by definition, not a measurement, so there is no uncertainty to carry. I read the B3 resolution PDF, whose endnote 4 restates B2: 'a conventional unit of length equal to 149 597 870 700 m exactly'. The code value is that number in km with no rounding loss.
source: IAU 2012 Resolution B2 (XXVIII General Assembly, Beijing); text restated verbatim in IAU 2015 Resolution B3, endnote 4 (arXiv:1510.07674, p.6)
your_value: 149597870.7 km (1 au = 149 597 870 700 m, exact by definition)

cited: IAU 2015 Resolution B3 -- nominal solar radius
notes: Matches to all digits. One thing worth carrying downstream: this is a conversion constant, not the measured photospheric radius. B3 endnote 2 gives the measurement as 695658 +/- 140 km (Haberreiter et al. 2008), and B3 explicitly says these nominal values 'should not be considered the true solar/planetary properties'. Every constant in this file expressed in R_sun inherits the nominal definition, which is the right choice for reproducibility.
source: IAU 2015 Resolution B3, Solar Conversion Constants table (Prsa et al. 2016, AJ 152:41; resolution text arXiv:1510.07674)
your_value: 695700 km (R_sun^N = 6.957e8 m, exact)

cited: IAU 2015 Resolution B3 -- nominal terrestrial equatorial radius
notes: The number is a standard, defensible value for Earth's equatorial radius. The citation is where this row is off. IAU 2015 B3 states R_eE^N = 6.3781e6 m -- five significant figures, 6378.1 km. It does not state 6378.137. The three extra digits come from IERS/WGS84, not from B3, so as written the row claims a precision its cited authority does not supply. B3 endnote 6 says the parameter 'corresponds to' the IERS zero-tide radius, which is how the two are related, but corresponding is not stating. Note the inconsistency is internal to the file: the polar-radius row immediately below cites IERS Conventions and even flags that B3 rounds to 6356.8. Cheapest fix is to make this row look like that one -- cite IERS Conventions 2010 or Archinal et al. 2018 Table 4 as the source of 6378.137, and mention B3's 6378.1 as the nominal conversion constant.
source: IAU 2015 Resolution B3, Planetary Conversion Constants table (arXiv:1510.07674); Archinal et al. 2018, CeMDA 130:22, Table 4; IERS Conventions 2010 (Petit & Luzum, IERS Technical Note 36)
your_value: 6378.1 km per the authority cited (R_eE^N = 6.3781e6 m, exact). The number 6378.137 km is the WGS84/GRS80 semi-major axis (6378137.0 m exactly); IERS Conventions 2010 give the zero-tide equatorial radius as 6378136.6 m, and Archinal et al. 2018 Table 4 gives 6378.1366 +/- 0.0001 km.

cited: IERS Conventions (Petit & Luzum 2010); IAU B3 rounds to 6356.8 km
notes: Verified against the WGCCRE table rather than the code: 6356.7519 km, which rounds to the code value. This row's citation is the model the equatorial row should follow: it names the authority that actually carries the digits and notes separately what the nominal standard says.
source: Archinal et al. 2018, CeMDA 130:22, Table 4 (size and shape parameters of the planets); IERS Conventions 2010 (Petit & Luzum, IERS Technical Note 36); IAU 2015 Resolution B3 for the nominal value
your_value: 6356.752 km (Archinal et al. 2018 Table 4: 6356.7519 +/- 0.0001 km; WGS84 semi-minor axis 6356752.314 m; IAU B3 nominal R_pE^N = 6.3568e6 m)

cited: NIST/SI exact definition
notes: Exact by definition of the metre, so the digits are not a measurement and cannot drift. Strictly the defining authority is the CGPM/BIPM and NIST is the publisher, but 'NIST/SI exact definition' names both correctly and the linked NIST page is the right place to land.
source: SI definition of the metre, 17th CGPM (1983) Resolution 1, carried into the 2019 SI; NIST CODATA reference value page for c (https://physics.nist.gov/cgi-bin/cuu/Value?c), listed with no uncertainty

cited: Carroll & Ostlie, An Introduction to Modern Astrophysics, Ch. 11 -- chromosphere extends ~2000 km above the photosphere.
notes: The number is a conventional round figure, not a constant. The chromosphere has no sharp outer boundary and its quoted thickness varies by a factor of several with the definition, so 2000 km is fine for a visualization shell but should not be carried as though it were determinate; a comment saying 'nominal quiet-Sun value' would cost one line and prevent someone later adding digits to it. On the citation: I could not consult Carroll & Ostlie, which is a print textbook I have no access to, so I cannot confirm Ch. 11 states 2000 km. Third-party lecture notes on that chapter quote ~2100 km for a chromospheric boundary height, which is consistent but is not the same number. Treat this citation as plausible and unchecked rather than verified -- and note that I am reporting a search I actually performed and could not complete, which is a different thing from having no verdict.
source: Standard solar-physics usage traceable to the VAL semi-empirical models (Vernazza, Avrett & Loeser 1981, ApJS 45:635). Representative refereed statements of ~2000 km: arXiv:2011.13469 sec.1 ('about 2,000 km thick'); arXiv:0902.3174 sec.1.2 ('above quiet Sun regions the chromosphere can be about 2 000 km thick'). For contrast, NASA's eclipse2017 science page gives ~5000 km.
your_value: ~2000 km is the standard quiet-Sun figure. There is no determinate value: published thicknesses run from a few hundred km to ~10000 km depending on whether spicules and the transition region are counted.

cited: Golub & Pasachoff, "The Solar Corona" (2010)
notes: 3 R_sun is a defensible shell boundary and it nests sensibly with the 6 R_sun streamer shell -- together they bracket the 1.5-6 R_sun middle-corona band the reviews use. But it is a drawing convention, and the reviews I consulted put the inner/middle transition closer to 1.5-2 R_sun. On the citation: Golub & Pasachoff, 'The Solar Corona', 2nd ed. (Cambridge, 2010) is a real book and the right authority for this material, but it is print-only and I could not consult it, so I cannot confirm it states 3 R_sun. Same caveat as the chromosphere row: this is a search performed and not completed, not an absent verdict.
source: 'Defining the Middle Corona', Solar Physics (2023), doi:10.1007/s11207-023-02170-1 (middle corona ~1.5-6 R_sun); 'The Sun's dynamic extended corona observed in extreme ultraviolet', Nature Astronomy (2021), doi:10.1038/s41550-021-01427-8 (describes the region as 1.5-3 R_sun)
your_value: No unique value; this is a naming convention rather than a measurement. Current reviews place the 'middle corona' at roughly 1.5-6 R_sun, which puts the outer edge of the inner corona nearer 1.5-3 R_sun than at 3 exactly.

cited: Golub & Pasachoff (2010); DeForest, Howard & McComas (2014), ApJ 787:124
context_only: See: Eclipse observations; helmet streamers extend 4-6 R_sun
notes: This is the row I would look at first. DeForest, Howard & McComas (2014) does not support '4-6 R_sun' for streamers. The 6 in that paper is the INNER radius beyond which they first detected inbound wave motion; the paper's actual streamer-belt number is a lower bound of 17 R_sun on the Alfven surface, with 12.5 over the polar holes. So a bounding figure has been taken from the wrong end of the result, and the direction of the error matters: the paper's point is that the relevant structure extends much further out than 6, not that it stops there. The value itself survives -- 6 R_sun is a reasonable choice for the top of the closed helmet structure, and it is the outer edge of the conventional middle-corona band -- but it survives independently of the citation attached to it. Golub & Pasachoff (2010) I could not consult. I would either re-cite this to a streamer-cusp reference or drop the DeForest citation from this row; note it is the same paper cited on the Alfven-surface row, where it does belong.
source: DeForest, Howard & McComas 2014, ApJ 787:124, abstract (arXiv:1404.3235): inbound wave motion identified beyond 6 R_sun, Alfven surface at least 12.5 R_sun over the polar coronal holes and 17 R_sun in the streamer belt. 'Defining the Middle Corona', Solar Physics (2023), doi:10.1007/s11207-023-02170-1, for the 1.5-6 R_sun band.
your_value: No single published value. Helmet-streamer cusps are conventionally placed at ~2-6 R_sun, but streamer structure is traced continuously outward through the COR2/LASCO fields of view to 15-30 R_sun. DeForest et al. (2014) gives no streamer extent at all; its streamer-belt result is a lower bound of >=17 R_sun on the Alfven surface.

cited: Murray & Dermott, "Solar System Dynamics" (1999), Sec. 4.6
context_only: Derived: Fluid Roche limit formula: d = 2.44 * R * (rho_sun/rho_comet)^(1/3)
Calculation: 2.44 * 1.0 * (1408/500)^(1/3) = 3.45 R_sun Using rho_sun = 1408 kg/m3, rho_comet ~ 500 kg/m3
notes: The arithmetic is right and the formula is the fluid form rather than the rigid-body form (coefficient 2.44 vs 1.26), which is the appropriate choice for a comet. But the output is only as good as rho_comet = 500 kg/m3, and that is an assumption, not a measurement: 67P/Churyumov-Gerasimenko, the only nucleus with a directly measured bulk density, is 533 kg/m3, and cometary densities span roughly 200-600. At 200 the limit moves to 4.7 R_sun; at 600 it moves to 3.2. So this is a scenario parameter wearing the clothes of a constant, and the assumed density belongs somewhere a reader will see it, not only in the derivation comment. On the citation: Murray & Dermott, 'Solar System Dynamics' (Cambridge, 1999) is the right book, but I could not consult it and cannot confirm the Roche limit is treated in Sec. 4.6 specifically.
source: Standard fluid (deformable-satellite) Roche limit d = 2.44 R_M (rho_M/rho_m)^(1/3); rho_sun = 1408 kg/m3 from the NASA NSSDCA Sun Fact Sheet (mean density).
your_value: 3.446 R_sun, which rounds to the code value. I reproduced the stated calculation: 2.44 * (1408/500)^(1/3) = 3.4456.

cited: Kasper et al. (2021), Phys. Rev. Lett. 127:255101
context_only: See: Parker Solar Probe first crossing, April 28, 2021
notes: Origin mismatch, and it is checkable. Both the PRL abstract and the NASA/APL release measure from the PHOTOSPHERE, not from Sun centre. The tell is internal to this file: the PARKER_CLOSEST_RADII row uses 9.86, which IS heliocentric -- the mission's 3.8 million miles above the surface is 8.86 R_sun of altitude and 9.86 from centre. So two constants in the same file, describing the same spacecraft, use different origins, and they differ by exactly 1 R_sun. If ALFVEN_SURFACE_RADII is drawn as a shell from Sun centre alongside HELIOPAUSE_RADII and PARKER_CLOSEST_RADII, it is low by one solar radius and should be 19.8. On the citation: Kasper et al. 2021 is the right paper for the event but does not itself print '18.8 solar radii' -- that figure comes from the press release, so the row cites the paper for a number only the release states. Two further cautions if this is drawn as a sphere: the crossing was into a low-Mach-number boundary layer above a pseudostreamer, not a global surface, and later PSP work finds the Alfven surface typically 10-20 R_sun, non-spherical, and expanding with rising solar activity.
source: Kasper et al. 2021, Phys. Rev. Lett. 127:255101, abstract ('entered the magnetized atmosphere of the Sun 13 million km above the photosphere'); NASA/Johns Hopkins APL news release, 14 December 2021, '18.8 solar radii (8.127 million miles) above the solar surface'.
your_value: 18.8 R_sun is correct as an ALTITUDE above the photosphere, not as a heliocentric radius. The first crossing was at ~19.8 R_sun from Sun centre: Kasper et al. 2021 state 13 million km above the photosphere (18.7 R_sun of altitude, 19.7 from centre), and the NASA/APL release's 8.127 million miles = 13.08 million km = 18.80 R_sun of altitude, hence 19.80 from centre.

cited: Stone et al. (2005), Science 309:2017
context_only: Also: Voyager 2 crossed at 84 AU (Aug 2007) -- asymmetric
notes: The abstract gives 94.01 au on 16 December 2004; Decker et al. 2005 (Science 309:2020) independently give 94.0 au. Value and citation both hold. The code's own comment already carries the right caveat, and it is worth keeping: this is one crossing of a moving, asymmetric boundary rather than a radius -- Voyager 2 crossed at ~84 au in August 2007, and the shock breathes in and out with solar wind ram pressure.
source: Stone et al. 2005, Science 309(5743):2017-2020, 'Voyager 1 Explores the Termination Shock Region and the Heliosheath Beyond', abstract
your_value: 94 AU (94.01 au, 16 December 2004)

cited: Gurnett et al. (2013), Science 341:1489
context_only: See: Voyager 1 crossed heliopause at ~121.6 AU (Aug 2012)
notes: The conversion is exact and reproduces the code value to the digit. Two cautions, neither fatal. First, precision: 121.6 au carries four significant figures and published values for the same crossing run 121.6-122 au, so the derived quantity is good to roughly +/-20 R_sun and the five-digit 26148 looks firmer than its input. Storing 121.6 and converting at use would be more honest than storing 26148. Second, as with the termination shock, this is a single crossing of an asymmetric, breathing boundary and not a heliopause radius -- Voyager 2 crossed at ~119 au in November 2018 on a different heading.
source: Gurnett et al. 2013, Science 341:1489, for the crossing; the distance 121.6 au is the figure conventionally attributed to it, e.g. 'Termination Shock Measured by Voyagers and IBEX', ApJ (2019), doi:10.3847/1538-4357/ab441a ('Voyager 1 crossed the heliopause and entered interstellar space at 121.6 au in 2012'). Conversion uses IAU 2012 B2 and the IAU 2015 B3 nominal solar radius.

cited: https://parkersolarprobe.jhuapl.edu/The-Mission/index.php
context_only: See: Parker Solar Probe perihelion 22, Dec 24, 2024
notes: Consistent from two directions, which is what makes it trustworthy: the WISPR instrument paper states the design perihelion as 9.86 R_sun from Sun centre, and the mission's 3.8 million miles above the surface converts to 8.86 R_sun of altitude, i.e. 9.86 from centre. Perihelion 22 on 24 December 2024 is correctly identified as the first pass at this distance; two more followed, on 22 March and 19 June 2025. This row is also the internal evidence that the file's convention is heliocentric, which is what makes the Alfven-surface row's 18.8 stand out. On the citation: the cited URL is the right mission authority but I did not fetch that specific page and cannot confirm it prints 9.86, and a bare mission-site index page with no section or retrieval date is a thin citation for a page that changes -- the WISPR paper would hold the number permanently.
source: 'The Wide-Field Imager for Solar Probe Plus (WISPR)', Space Science Reviews, doi:10.1007/s11214-014-0114-y, which states the mission will orbit 'as close as 7 million km (9.86 solar radii) from Sun center'; NASA/JHU-APL release 'Parker Solar Probe Makes History With Closest Pass to the Sun', 27 December 2024, for the 3.8 million miles above the surface on 24 December 2024.
your_value: 9.86 R_sun heliocentric (6.86 million km from Sun centre; equivalently 6.1 million km / 3.8 million miles above the photosphere)

cited: Nolan et al. 2013 (radar shape model), mean diameter 492 +/- 20 m Confirmed by OSIRIS-REx OLA: mean radius 246 +/- 10 m, V = 0.062 km^3
notes: The code value is the pre-encounter radar figure. Nolan et al. 2013 gave a mean diameter of 492 +/- 20 m, half of which is the 246 m carried here; OSIRIS-REx superseded it with 490.06 +/- 0.16 m, i.e. 245.0 m. The 0.4 percent difference is irrelevant to a display, but the third decimal in 0.246 is now wrong and should be 0.245. The citation needs more attention than the value: the comment attributes 'mean radius 246 +/- 10 m, V = 0.062 km3' to OSIRIS-REx OLA, and those are not OLA's numbers -- they are the Nolan radar numbers again (0.062 +/- 0.006 km3 was the pre-encounter volume, and +/-10 m is half the radar's +/-20 m diameter uncertainty). OLA and SPC give 0.061354 and 0.0615 km3 with uncertainties around 0.1 percent, not 4 percent. The substance of the claim is true -- OLA did confirm the radar result within its uncertainty -- but the figures attached to the confirmation are the ones being confirmed, not the confirming ones, which makes the row read as though the mission independently produced 246 +/- 10.
source: Barnouin et al. 2019, Nature Geoscience 12:247-252, doi:10.1038/s41561-019-0330-x ('GDTM has a volume of 0.0615 +/- 0.0001 km3'); Daly et al. 2020, OLA-based GDTM volume 0.061354 km3; Lauretta et al. 2019 mean diameter 490.06 +/- 0.16 m, as quoted in Barucci et al. 2020, A&A 637:L4.
your_value: 0.2450 km. Lauretta et al. 2019 give a mean diameter of 490.06 +/- 0.16 m (mean radius 245.03 m), and the Barnouin et al. 2019 global DTM volume of 0.0615 +/- 0.0001 km3 gives an equivalent-sphere radius of 244.9 m.

cited: JPL SSD mean radius (Lockwood et al. 2014) Highly ellipsoidal: 1050x840x537 km -> geometric mean 779.5 km JPL SSD publishes 715; equatorial 870
notes: The largest disagreement in the batch. 715 km is not fabricated -- it is exactly the volume-equivalent radius of the Lockwood et al. 2014 hydrostatic model the row cites, and I reproduced it to the digit -- but that model was overturned by the 2017 stellar occultation, which is the only direct size measurement of Haumea. The occultation puts the mean radius near 798 km: 11 percent larger in radius, 39 percent larger in volume. Reanalyses of the same event that relax the rotational-phase assumption land around 772-798 km, so the honest answer is a range, and every value in it is well above 715. Separately, the dimensions in the comment, 1050 x 840 x 537 km, match neither cited model: Lockwood gives semi-axes 960 x 770 x 495 and Ortiz gives 1161 x 852 x 513. I could not find any published shape model with 1050 x 840 x 537 and cannot account for where it came from. That is worth tracing rather than just correcting, because '-> geometric mean 779.5 km' computes correctly FROM those axes -- somebody did valid arithmetic on a set of numbers with no source, which is a different failure from a typo and may have a sibling elsewhere in the corpus. Finally, a single radius is a poor summary of this object at all: its long axis is more than twice its short axis.
source: Ortiz et al. 2017, Nature, 'The size, shape, density and ring of the dwarf planet Haumea from a stellar occultation' (arXiv:2006.03113); Dunham et al. 2019, 'Haumea's Shape, Composition, and Internal Structure', doi:10.3847/1538-4357/ab13b3 ('the mean radius of Haumea is larger at 798 km'); Lockwood et al. 2014 semi-axes as quoted in Muller et al., arXiv:1904.06333, sec. 3.2.
your_value: ~798 km volume-equivalent mean radius, from the only direct measurement. Ortiz et al. 2017 give semi-axes 1161 +/- 30 x 852 +/- 4 x 513 +/- 16 km; (1161*852*513)^(1/3) = 797.6 km, and Dunham et al. 2019 state the mean radius as 798 km. The code's 715 is the Lockwood et al. 2014 model: their semi-axes 960 x 770 x 495 km give (960*770*495)^(1/3) = 715.3 km.

cited: Keane et al. 2022, JGR Planets (New Horizons shape model) Volume 3166 km^3 -> equivalent sphere radius 9.1 km Overall dims 35.95 x 19.90 x 9.75 km (bilobed contact binary) Corrected 2026-04-15 per Gemini review (was 0.0088 = 8.8 meters!)
notes: Two things, one of which postdates the correction noted in the comment. First, there is now a newer shape model: the New Horizons KEM2 reanalysis is explicitly 'significantly thicker and of larger volume' than Spencer et al. 2020, and gives a volume-equivalent mean radius of 9.95 km against 9.1. That is a 9 percent change and it moves in the opposite direction from the 2026-04-15 correction, so this row has now been wrong in both directions and is worth a watch flag rather than another one-time fix. Second, on attribution: I confirmed that Keane et al. 2022 is the source of the 35.95 x 19.90 x 9.75 dimensions, and that its two lobe volumes sum to roughly 3.1e3 km3, consistent with 3166. But the specific figure 3166 km3 and the phrase 'equivalent to a sphere of radius 9.1 km' I found verbatim in Amarante & Winter (2022), working from the Spencer et al. 2020 model, not in Keane. I did not read Keane et al. 2022 in full and cannot rule out that it states 3166 as well; what I can say is that the number's traceable published home is a different paper. The arithmetic in the comment checks out either way.
source: Keane et al. 2022, JGR Planets 127:e2021JE007068, doi:10.1029/2021JE007068 (overall dimensions 35.95 x 19.90 x 9.75 km; lobe volumes ~1.98e12 and ~1.10e12 m3, summing to ~3.1e3 km3). The figure 3166 km3 with 'equivalent to a sphere of radius 9.1 km' appears in Amarante & Winter 2022, arXiv:2203.14444, sec. 2.1, applied to the Spencer et al. 2020 shape model. Porter et al., 'The Shape of (486958) Arrokoth', arXiv:2605.30069 and the New Horizons PDS release, for the updated model.
your_value: 9.1 km for the shape model the row cites -- volume 3166 km3 gives (3V/4pi)^(1/3) = 9.109 km, which I reproduced. The current model gives ~9.95 km: Porter et al. report overall dimensions 34.546 x 19.838 x 13.822 km and a volume-equivalent mean diameter of 19.896 km.
